Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

have verb

own, possess

also have got, I have, has, had, own

classical

Phaedr. 4.25.16–21: cum opus est, nīl habēs

habeō, habēre, habuī, habitum

verb, second conjugation

The plain word for having a thing. It does not stretch as far as English “have”: one does not habēre a meal, a bath, a baby or a look; Latin names the action (prandēre, lavārī, parere, aspicere).

Other words

  • est mihi — I have (literally “there is to me”)

    phrase: the owner in the dative, the thing owned as the subject of esse · classical · Mart. 11.18.2: rūs est mihi majus in fenestrā

    As common as habeō, and the usual way with family, a name and qualities: est mihi frāter, I have a brother; nōmen mihi est …, my name is …

Examples

  • dōnāstī, Lupe, rūs sub urbe nōbīs; sed rūs est mihi majus in fenestrā

    you gave me a farm outside town, Lupus; but I have a bigger farm in my windowMart. 11.18.1–2

  • nihil labōrās? ideō, cum opus est, nīl habēs

    you do no work? That is why you have nothing when you need itPhaedr. 4.25.16–21

See also have, own, own, there is.
